name: Somali Sambuus (Beef Sambusa)
imageAlt: Plate of triangular Somali sambuus fried until golden
imageCredit: Photo: La.Catholique, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
summary: Somali sambuus filled with finely crumbled beef, onion, garlic, green chile and warm spice, sealed into thin triangular wrappers and fried until crisp and blistered.
lead: These crisp Somali sambuus are built around a dry, highly seasoned beef filling and a thin wrapper that fries quickly without turning greasy.
about: Somali writer Ifrah F. Ahmed describes sambuus as celebration food strongly associated with weddings, Ramadan and Eid, while also placing it within a broader East African and Middle Eastern family of filled pastries shaped by centuries of trade and migration. PBS documentation of Somali cooks making sambusa likewise emphasizes the thin handmade wrapper, finely broken-up meat filling and the importance of the triangular fold. This home version keeps that structure and uses a beef filling seasoned with garlic, onion, chile, coriander and cumin.
story: Sambuus should not be reduced to a generic samosa with a Somali label. Somali families have their own wrapper techniques, fillings, spice preferences and serving customs, and Ahmed writes about the pastry as a carrier of memory, migration and community identity. Ramadan is an especially important context: sambuus often appears when the daily fast is broken, but it also belongs at weddings, family gatherings and tea tables. Diaspora kitchens may use tortillas or commercial wrappers for convenience; this recipe instead follows the thin flour-wrapper tradition while keeping the method manageable at home.
caveat: Beef is common, but Somali sambuus may also be filled with lamb, fish, vegetables or other household fillings. A commercial spring-roll wrapper is a practical substitute, but it produces a different texture from the layered handmade wrapper described by Somali cooks. Keep the filling dry and cool before wrapping; excess liquid is the main cause of splitting and greasy pastry.
prepNotes: Continue cooking after the beef is browned until no watery liquid collects in the pan. A dry filling protects the wrapper and keeps the finished pastry crisp.
Warm filling softens the dough and creates steam pockets that can burst in hot oil.
Use a flour-and-water paste and inspect each triangle for gaps before frying. Even a small opening can leak filling into the oil.
ingredients: 3/4 cup warm water, plus more as needed
2 tbsp all-purpose flour mixed with 2 tbsp water, for sealing paste
1/2 green bell pepper, very finely diced
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
Lemon wedges or green basbaas-style chile sauce, for serving
steps: Mix the flour and 1/2 teaspoon salt. Add 2 tablespoons oil and most of the warm water, then knead 6 to 8 minutes until the dough is smooth, soft and no longer shaggy. Add the remaining water only if the dough feels stiff.
Cover the dough and rest 25 minutes. Checkpoint: after resting, it should roll thin without snapping back aggressively and should feel supple rather than sticky.

Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Add the beef and break it into very fine crumbles. Cook 5 to 7 minutes until no pink remains and the pan begins to sound like frying rather than simmering.
Add onion, garlic, ginger, coriander, cumin, black pepper, chile and bell pepper. Cook 5 to 7 minutes more, stirring often, until the onion is soft and any released liquid has evaporated.

Checkpoint: drag a spoon through the filling. The pan should stay visibly dry for several seconds, the beef should smell toasted and warmly spiced, and there should be no puddle collecting around the meat.
Remove from the heat, fold in scallions and cilantro, season with 1 teaspoon salt and spread the filling on a tray to cool completely.

Divide the dough into 8 balls. Roll each ball into a very thin 7-inch round. Lightly oil one round, dust with flour, top with a second round and roll the pair together slightly thinner. Repeat to make 4 paired rounds.

Dry-cook each paired round in a hot skillet for about 20 to 30 seconds per side, just until the surfaces set but do not brown deeply. Separate the two layers while still warm, then cut each circle in half to make 16 semicircular wrappers.

Form each semicircle into a cone, sealing the overlapping edge with flour paste. Add about 2 tablespoons cooled filling, leaving enough empty wrapper to close the top. Paint the final edge with paste and press firmly into a triangle.
Heat 2 inches of oil to 350°F. Fry 3 to 4 sambuus at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until evenly deep golden and visibly blistered.
Checkpoint: maintain roughly 340°F to 355°F. If the pastries darken in under 2 minutes the oil is too hot; if they sit pale and absorb oil, let the temperature recover before the next batch.
Drain on a rack rather than stacking. Rest 3 minutes before serving so the crust stays crisp and the beef filling is hot but not scalding.
sources: Los Angeles Times - Ifrah F. Ahmed on Somali sambuus, Ramadan, Eid and migration
PBS Relish - Somali Sambusa and Nepali Momo

name: Azerbaijani Badambura
imageAlt: Layered Azerbaijani badambura pastries filled with almond and cardamom
imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons: Badambura 1.JPG; reuse under the license listed on the file page.
summary: Azerbaijani badambura made from thin buttered layers of enriched dough wrapped around almond, sugar and cardamom, baked pale and finished with powdered sugar.
lead: Badambura hides an almond-cardamom filling inside dozens of visible pastry layers, with a pale shell that is tender, flaky and fragrant rather than deeply browned.
about: Azerbaijan's national tourism site describes badambura as a popular traditional sweet served for Novruz, weddings and tea, and gives its defining structure as layered dough filled with almonds, sugar and cardamom. The same official recipe specifically instructs cooks to bake at a low enough temperature that the pastries stay pale. This scaled home version preserves that almond-cardamom center and the coiled laminated shape while reducing the very large festival proportions to a dozen pastries.
story: Badambura belongs to Azerbaijan's broader culture of festive pastries, where nuts, cardamom, butter and careful shaping appear across sweets served with tea and during Novruz. It is visually distinct because stacked, buttered sheets are rolled into a log, sliced to expose concentric layers, then opened into a small cup for filling. The target is not croissant-like expansion or a dark bakery crust; the pastry is traditionally kept comparatively pale so the layered pattern remains delicate and the almond-cardamom aroma stays central.
caveat: Walnuts or hazelnuts can make a pleasant filled pastry, but they change the specific almond profile described in Azerbaijan's tourism recipe and should not be presented as identical. Ground cardamom is essential to the traditional flavor. Do not increase the oven heat simply to force browning; a pale finish is part of the documented style.
prepNotes: The visible spiral depends on many thin layers. Aim for sheets thin enough to become slightly translucent without tearing.
Keep the butter soft, not hot
Melted-hot butter can soak into the dough instead of keeping layers distinct. Use softened or barely melted butter.
Badambura should bake through while remaining ivory to light gold. A dark brown surface means the oven is too hot or the pastries have baked too long.
ingredients: 3 1/2 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for rolling
6 tbsp unsalted butter, softened, for the dough
8 tbsp unsalted butter, very soft or barely melted, for layering
steps: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt. Add sour cream, egg, warm milk and 6 tablespoons softened butter. Knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Cover and let rise 45 to 60 minutes in a warm place. Checkpoint: the dough should look visibly fuller and an indentation should spring back slowly, but it does not need to fully double.
Mix ground almonds, 3/4 cup sugar and cardamom. Rub a spoonful between your fingers; it should smell distinctly floral and nutty, with no large almond chunks that could tear the dough.
Divide the risen dough into 6 equal pieces. Roll each into a very thin rectangle, roughly 10 by 14 inches, keeping the work surface lightly floured.
Lay the first sheet flat and brush it lightly but completely with layering butter. Stack the second sheet on top and repeat until all 6 layers are stacked and buttered except the very top.
Roll the stacked sheets tightly from a long side into a compact log. Chill 20 minutes so the butter firms enough for clean slicing.

Cut the log crosswise into 12 equal rounds. Place each cut side up and gently press the center down with both thumbs while supporting the outer rings, opening it into a small layered cup without crushing the spiral.
Add about 2 tablespoons almond filling. Pinch the opening closed securely, then place seam-side down on a parchment-lined tray. The layered spiral should remain visible on top.

Bake at 325°F for 28 to 35 minutes, rotating the tray once. Checkpoint: the bottoms should be set and lightly golden, the tops should remain pale ivory to very light gold, and the pastry layers should feel dry rather than doughy when gently tapped.
Cool 10 minutes, then dust with powdered sugar. Let the pastries finish cooling before storing so trapped steam does not soften the layers.
sources: Azerbaijan Travel - Badambura recipe and festival context
AramcoWorld - Tastes of Azerbaijan and regional pastry/foodways context

name: Newari Chatamari
imageAlt: Newari meat chatamari on a thin rice-flour base
imageCredit: Photo: Raunak Maskay, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
summary: Newari chatamari from the Kathmandu Valley: a thin rice-flour batter spread on a hot pan and cooked covered until the base is set and lightly crisp, with meat and egg as documented variations.
lead: Chatamari starts with a simple rice-flour batter and becomes a highly adaptable Newari pan bread, from plain versions served with curry to meat-and-egg topped forms cooked under a lid.
about: The Nepal Tourism Board's heritage cuisine recipe book identifies chatamari by its Newari name and gives a plain rice-flour batter method cooked on an iron pan under a lid, with egg, cheese, meat or vegetables documented as variations. That source is useful because it keeps the dish rooted in Newar food culture while also acknowledging its wider popularity in Nepal. This version uses a thin meat-and-egg topping inspired by documented Kathmandu Valley practice while keeping the rice base crisp at the edges and tender through the center.
story: Chatamari is sometimes marketed as 'Nepali pizza,' but that nickname can hide the technique that actually defines it. The base is a rice-flour batter, not a risen wheat dough, and the covered-pan method cooks the top with trapped steam while the bottom sets against a hot iron surface. Newari versions range from plain to topped with egg, minced meat, vegetables or cheese. Rather than treating one topping combination as definitive, this recipe presents meat and egg as one documented branch of a larger Newar preparation.
caveat: Do not substitute wheat flour one-for-one for rice flour; it changes both the structure and identity of the base. Buffalo meat is used in many Newari meat preparations, but ground beef is a practical home substitute where buffalo is unavailable and is labeled as such here. A plain chatamari without meat or egg is also fully legitimate and is the form documented in the Nepal Tourism Board base recipe.
prepNotes: The batter should spread under gentle wrist movement but not run like water. Resting it briefly hydrates the rice flour and reduces cracking.
Raw meat must be spread in a very thin layer so it cooks safely in the few minutes the base spends under the lid.
Too much heat scorches the rice base before the steam can set the topping; too little leaves the base pale and rubbery.
ingredients: Neutral oil or mustard oil, for greasing the pan
10 oz ground buffalo or ground beef as a practical substitute
3/4 tsp kosher salt, for the topping
3 large eggs, lightly beaten, or 6 small eggs for one per chatamari
Tomato or achar-style chile pickle, for serving, optional
steps: Whisk rice flour and 1/2 teaspoon salt with 1 3/4 cups warm water until completely smooth. Let the batter rest 15 minutes, then whisk again and add enough remaining water to reach a consistency slightly thinner than pancake batter.
Checkpoint: lift the whisk. The batter should fall in a steady ribbon and disappear back into the bowl within a few seconds without leaving lumps.
Mix the ground meat with onion, scallion, ginger, garlic, cumin, coriander, chile, 3/4 teaspoon salt and cilantro. Keep the mixture chilled until the pan is ready.
Heat a well-seasoned cast-iron or nonstick skillet over medium-high heat, then wipe with a very thin film of oil. A drop of batter should sizzle gently on contact rather than blacken.
Pour about 1/3 cup batter into the center and immediately tilt or spread it into a thin 7-inch circle. Lower the heat to medium.
For a meat version, scatter a very thin layer of seasoned meat over the still-wet surface, leaving a narrow border. Spoon a little beaten egg over the meat, or crack one small egg into the center.
Cover tightly and cook 4 to 6 minutes. Do not flip unless the topping is unusually thick. The lid traps the steam needed to cook the upper surface.

Checkpoint: the rice base should release from the pan at the edges and show light golden patches underneath; the egg white should be fully opaque; and ground meat must reach at least 160°F in several spots.
Uncover and cook 30 to 60 seconds more if you want a crisper edge. Slide the chatamari onto a plate rather than folding it while hot.
Repeat with the remaining batter, wiping the pan lightly with oil between rounds and adjusting heat as needed. Serve immediately with achar or a curry-based meat or vegetable accompaniment.
sources: Nepal Tourism Board - Experience Nepal heritage cuisine recipe book: Chatamari
Wikimedia Commons - Meat Chatamari by Raunak Maskay, Kathmandu Valley
